**Answer:**  
The place where Pope Pius XI died – the Apostolic Palace in Rome – lies inside what is today Vatican City. Vatican City became an independent, sovereign country on **11 February 1929**, when the Lateran Pacts signed by the Holy See and Italy formally established the State of Vatican City. Thus, the place of death of the author of *Quadragesimo Anno* became its own country in 1929.

**Pius XI** (1857–1939) was pope from February 1922 until his death in February 1939. Born Achille Ratti near Milan, he was a scholar-librarian and diplomat before becoming archbishop of Milan and then pope. He is remembered most for the Lateran Pacts of 1929, which settled the long dispute between the papacy and the Italian state and created the State of Vatican City. He also gave Roman Catholic social teaching a new statement in _Quadragesimo anno_ (1931), promoted lay involvement through Catholic Action, and signed agreements with many governments. He condemned Italian Fascism's treatment of the church, German National Socialism, and atheistic communism, and he advanced native leadership in the Catholic missions of Asia.

## Early life and career
Ambrogio Damiano Achille Ratti was born on May 31, 1857, at Desio, a town north of Milan, the son of a manager in the silk industry. He studied for the priesthood in Milan and was ordained in 1879. Further study in Rome earned him three doctorates, in philosophy, theology, and canon law.
For most of his working life Ratti was a scholar. From 1888 he served at the Ambrosian Library in Milan, one of Italy's great collections of manuscripts, and became its prefect in 1907. He edited and published historical documents, especially records relating to the church in Milan. In 1911 he moved to the Vatican Library in Rome, and in 1914 he became its prefect. He was also a serious mountaineer who made notable ascents in the Alps, including Monte Rosa and the Matterhorn.
In 1918 Pope Benedict XV sent him to Poland, newly restored as an independent state after World War I, first as apostolic visitor and then, from 1919, as papal nuncio (the pope's ambassador). He remained in Warsaw in 1920 when the Soviet Red Army advanced on the city, a decision that won him respect among the Poles. In 1921 Benedict made him archbishop of Milan and a cardinal. He had held the see only a few months when Benedict died in January 1922.

## Election and program
The conclave elected Ratti on February 6, 1922, after fourteen ballots. He took the name Pius. In a gesture that was widely noticed, he gave his first blessing from the outer balcony of St. Peter's Basilica, facing the city of Rome. His predecessors since 1870 had refused to do so as a protest against the Italian state's seizure of Rome.
His first encyclical, _Ubi arcano Dei consilio_ (December 1922), set out the theme of his reign in the motto "the peace of Christ in the reign of Christ." He argued that the disorders of the postwar world could be healed only when individuals, families, and nations submitted to Christ's rule. In 1925 he expressed the same idea liturgically by instituting the Feast of Christ the King in the encyclical _Quas primas_.

## The Lateran Pacts and Vatican City
The "Roman Question" had troubled relations between the papacy and Italy for decades. The Papal States, the territories in central Italy that the popes had ruled for more than a thousand years, were largely absorbed into the new Kingdom of Italy in 1859–60, and Rome itself was taken in 1870. The popes refused to accept the loss, would not recognize the Italian state, and regarded themselves as prisoners in the Vatican.
Pius XI resolved the matter by negotiation with the government of Benito Mussolini. The Lateran Pacts, signed on February 11, 1929, by Cardinal Pietro Gasparri for the Holy See and by Mussolini for Italy, had three parts. A treaty recognized the full sovereignty of the Holy See over a small territory of roughly 109 acres (44 hectares), the new State of Vatican City, and the papacy in turn recognized the Italian state with Rome as its capital. A concordat (a formal agreement on the church's legal position) recognized Roman Catholicism as the religion of the Italian state, gave church marriages civil effect, and provided for religious instruction in schools. A financial convention compensated the papacy for the territories it had lost.
The settlement gave the papacy a secure, internationally recognized base independent of any government. It also brought Mussolini's regime prestige and the goodwill of many Catholics at a crucial stage in its consolidation, and it has been debated ever since for that reason. The concordat remained in force until it was revised by a new agreement in 1984.

## Social teaching
On the fortieth anniversary of Leo XIII's encyclical _Rerum novarum_ (1891), Pius issued _Quadragesimo anno_ (May 15, 1931), "in the fortieth year." It restated and developed Catholic teaching on property, labor, and the economic order at the time of the Great Depression. It rejected both unrestrained economic individualism and socialism, and it criticized the concentration of economic power in a few hands.
The encyclical is best known for its statement of the principle of subsidiarity. On this principle, larger bodies, including the state, should not take over tasks that smaller communities such as families, associations, and local bodies can perform themselves; higher authority should support and assist the lower rather than absorb it. The encyclical also proposed that society be organized through vocational groups that would bring together employers and workers in each branch of the economy. Fascist Italy claimed that its own corporative system put similar ideas into practice, but the Italian state's corporations were tools of government control, and the encyclical itself voiced concern about that kind of arrangement.
Other encyclicals addressed family and education. _Divini illius magistri_ (1929) set out the Catholic understanding of Christian education, holding that the family and the church have rights in education that come before those of the state, and opposing a state monopoly over schooling. _Casti connubii_ (1930) defended the permanence of marriage and condemned artificial contraception, a teaching that later popes reaffirmed.

## Catholic Action and the laity
Pius XI made the organized lay movement known as Catholic Action a central feature of his program. He described it as the participation of the laity in the apostolate of the hierarchy: lay Catholics, organized by age, sex, and occupation, would work under the direction of the bishops to bring Christian principles into public life, the professions, and the workplace. The movement spread widely in Italy, Belgium, France, Latin America, and elsewhere.
Catholic Action became a point of conflict with the Fascist government, which wanted a monopoly over the organization of young people. When the regime moved against Catholic youth groups in 1931, Pius answered with the encyclical _Non abbiamo bisogno_ ("We do not need"), written in Italian rather than the customary Latin. In it he protested against the persecution of Catholic Action and rejected the claim of the totalitarian state to the whole of a young person's life. A compromise allowed the groups to continue under restrictions.

## Concordats and relations with states
Pius used concordats extensively to secure the church's legal position after World War I redrew the map of Europe. Agreements were reached with, among others, Latvia (1922), Bavaria (1924), Poland (1925), Lithuania (1927), Romania (1927), Prussia (1929), Italy (1929), Baden (1932), and Austria (1933). In July 1933 the Holy See signed a concordat with the German Reich, negotiated on the Vatican side by Cardinal Eugenio Pacelli, his secretary of state from 1930. It guaranteed certain rights to the church in Germany in exchange for the withdrawal of clergy from party politics. Historians continue to debate whether the agreement protected German Catholics or lent the new Nazi regime respectability; the regime in any case violated it repeatedly.
In France, diplomatic relations with the Holy See had been restored under Benedict XV in 1921, after a break of nearly two decades. Pius XI built on this by accepting, in 1924, a legal arrangement for French dioceses that allowed the church to hold property under the laws separating church and state. In 1926 he condemned the right-wing nationalist movement Action Française, whose Catholic supporters had made it a significant force in French Catholic life, because of its subordination of religion to politics.
The church faced open persecution in several countries during his reign. He protested against the anticlerical measures of the Mexican government that led to the Cristero uprising of 1926–29 and its aftermath, against the treatment of the church under the Spanish Republic and during the Spanish Civil War, and against the suppression of religion in the Soviet Union.

**Pius XI**
Pope Pius XI (1857-1939) (original name Ambrogio Damiano Achille Ratti) , was born in Desio, Lombardy, Austrian Empire [now in Italy]. His father owned a silk factory. He was ordained a priest in 1879 and embarked on an academic career within the Church. He obtained three doctorates (in philosophy, canon law and theology) at the Gregorian University in Rome, and then from 1882 to 1888 was a professor at the seminary in Padua. His scholarly specialty was as an expert paleographer, a student of ancient and medieval Church manuscripts. After many years as a researcher at a Catholic library, Ratti was made Papal nuncio to Poland in 1918, then cardinal and archbishop of Milan in 1921, and then Pope in the following year.
Among his papal encyclicals, Pius XI is most remembered for lending the support of the Church to Distributism and Subsidiarity in Quadragesimo Anno. It was promulgated in 1931 to mark ‘forty years’ since Pope Leo XIII’s (1878–1903) encyclical De Rerum Novarum. It restated that encyclical’s support for intermediating social associations and warnings against both socialism and unrestrained capitalism as enemies to human freedom and dignity.
The following excerpt defined the principle of subsidiarity that has been a feature of Catholic thought ever since:
“The State authorities should leave to other bodies the care and expediting of business and activities of lesser moment, which otherwise become for it a source of great distraction. It will then perform with greater freedom, vigor and effectiveness, the tasks belonging properly to it, and which alone it can accomplish, directing, supervising, encouraging, restraining, as circumstances suggest or necessity demands. Let those in power, therefore, be convinced that the more faithfully this principle of subsidiarity is followed and a hierarchical order prevails among the various organizations the more excellent will be the authority and efficiency of society, and the happier and more prosperous the condition of the commonwealth.”
**In Centesimus Annus (1991) John Paul II formulated the principle with a different emphasis:**

# Quadragesimo Anno
“A community of a higher order should not interfere in the internal life of a community of lower order, depriving the latter of its functions, but rather should support it in case of need and help to coordinate its activity with the activities of the rest of society, always with a view to the common good.”

He is remembered most for the Lateran Pacts of 1929, which settled the long dispute between the papacy and the Italian state and created the State of Vatican City. He also gave Roman Catholic social teaching a new statement in _Quadragesimo anno_ (1931), promoted lay involvement through Catholic Action, and signed agreements with many governments. He condemned Italian Fascism's treatment of the church, German National Socialism, and atheistic communism, and he advanced native leadership in the Catholic missions of Asia.
texts.1:
## Early life and career
Ambrogio Damiano Achille Ratti was born on May 31, 1857, at Desio, a town north of Milan, the son of a manager in the silk industry. He studied for the priesthood in Milan and was ordained in 1879. Further study in Rome earned him three doctorates, in philosophy, theology, and canon law.
For most of his working life Ratti was a scholar. From 1888 he served at the Ambrosian Library in Milan, one of Italy's great collections of manuscripts, and became its prefect in 1907. He edited and published historical documents, especially records relating to the church in Milan. In 1911 he moved to the Vatican Library in Rome, and in 1914 he became its prefect. He was also a serious mountaineer who made notable ascents in the Alps, including Monte Rosa and the Matterhorn.
In 1918 Pope Benedict XV sent him to Poland, newly restored as an independent state after World War I, first as apostolic visitor and then, from 1919, as papal nuncio (the pope's ambassador). He remained in Warsaw in 1920 when the Soviet Red Army advanced on the city, a decision that won him respect among the Poles. In 1921 Benedict made him archbishop of Milan and a cardinal. He had held the see only a few months when Benedict died in January 1922.
texts.2:
## Election and program
The conclave elected Ratti on February 6, 1922, after fourteen ballots. He took the name Pius. In a gesture that was widely noticed, he gave his first blessing from the outer balcony of St. Peter's Basilica, facing the city of Rome. His predecessors since 1870 had refused to do so as a protest against the Italian state's seizure of Rome.
His first encyclical, _Ubi arcano Dei consilio_ (December 1922), set out the theme of his reign in the motto "the peace of Christ in the reign of Christ." He argued that the disorders of the postwar world could be healed only when individuals, families, and nations submitted to Christ's rule. In 1925 he expressed the same idea liturgically by instituting the Feast of Christ the King in the encyclical _Quas primas_.
texts.3:
## The Lateran Pacts and Vatican City
The "Roman Question" had troubled relations between the papacy and Italy for decades. The Papal States, the territories in central Italy that the popes had ruled for more than a thousand years, were largely absorbed into the new Kingdom of Italy in 1859–60, and Rome itself was taken in 1870. The popes refused to accept the loss, would not recognize the Italian state, and regarded themselves as prisoners in the Vatican.
Pius XI resolved the matter by negotiation with the government of Benito Mussolini. The Lateran Pacts, signed on February 11, 1929, by Cardinal Pietro Gasparri for the Holy See and by Mussolini for Italy, had three parts. A treaty recognized the full sovereignty of the Holy See over a small territory of roughly 109 acres (44 hectares), the new State of Vatican City, and the papacy in turn recognized the Italian state with Rome as its capital. A concordat (a formal agreement on the church's legal position) recognized Roman Catholicism as the religion of the Italian state, gave church marriages civil effect, and provided for religious instruction in schools. A financial convention compensated the papacy for the territories it had lost.
The settlement gave the papacy a secure, internationally recognized base independent of any government. It also brought Mussolini's regime prestige and the goodwill of many Catholics at a crucial stage in its consolidation, and it has been debated ever since for that reason. The concordat remained in force until it was revised by a new agreement in 1984.
texts.4:
## Social teaching
On the fortieth anniversary of Leo XIII's encyclical _Rerum novarum_ (1891), Pius issued _Quadragesimo anno_ (May 15, 1931), "in the fortieth year." It restated and developed Catholic teaching on property, labor, and the economic order at the time of the Great Depression. It rejected both unrestrained economic individualism and socialism, and it criticized the concentration of economic power in a few hands.
The encyclical is best known for its statement of the principle of subsidiarity. On this principle, larger bodies, including the state, should not take over tasks that smaller communities such as families, associations, and local bodies can perform themselves; higher authority should support and assist the lower rather than absorb it. The encyclical also proposed that society be organized through vocational groups that would bring together employers and workers in each branch of the economy. Fascist Italy claimed that its own corporative system put similar ideas into practice, but the Italian state's corporations were tools of government control, and the encyclical itself voiced concern about that kind of arrangement.
Other encyclicals addressed family and education. _Divini illius magistri_ (1929) set out the Catholic understanding of Christian education, holding that the family and the church have rights in education that come before those of the state, and opposing a state monopoly over schooling. _Casti connubii_ (1930) defended the permanence of marriage and condemned artificial contraception, a teaching that later popes reaffirmed.
texts.5:
## Catholic Action and the laity
Pius XI made the organized lay movement known as Catholic Action a central feature of his program. He described it as the participation of the laity in the apostolate of the hierarchy: lay Catholics, organized by age, sex, and occupation, would work under the direction of the bishops to bring Christian principles into public life, the professions, and the workplace. The movement spread widely in Italy, Belgium, France, Latin America, and elsewhere.
Catholic Action became a point of conflict with the Fascist government, which wanted a monopoly over the organization of young people. When the regime moved against Catholic youth groups in 1931, Pius answered with the encyclical _Non abbiamo bisogno_ ("We do not need"), written in Italian rather than the customary Latin. In it he protested against the persecution of Catholic Action and rejected the claim of the totalitarian state to the whole of a young person's life. A compromise allowed the groups to continue under restrictions.
texts.6:
## Concordats and relations with states
Pius used concordats extensively to secure the church's legal position after World War I redrew the map of Europe. Agreements were reached with, among others, Latvia (1922), Bavaria (1924), Poland (1925), Lithuania (1927), Romania (1927), Prussia (1929), Italy (1929), Baden (1932), and Austria (1933). In July 1933 the Holy See signed a concordat with the German Reich, negotiated on the Vatican side by Cardinal Eugenio Pacelli, his secretary of state from 1930. It guaranteed certain rights to the church in Germany in exchange for the withdrawal of clergy from party politics. Historians continue to debate whether the agreement protected German Catholics or lent the new Nazi regime respectability; the regime in any case violated it repeatedly.
In France, diplomatic relations with the Holy See had been restored under Benedict XV in 1921, after a break of nearly two decades. Pius XI built on this by accepting, in 1924, a legal arrangement for French dioceses that allowed the church to hold property under the laws separating church and state. In 1926 he condemned the right-wing nationalist movement Action Française, whose Catholic supporters had made it a significant force in French Catholic life, because of its subordination of religion to politics.
The church faced open persecution in several countries during his reign. He protested against the anticlerical measures of the Mexican government that led to the Cristero uprising of 1926–29 and its aftermath, against the treatment of the church under the Spanish Republic and during the Spanish Civil War, and against the suppression of religion in the Soviet Union.

### The Death of Pius XI
Gregory DiPippo
Today marks the anniversary of the death of Pope Pius XI in 1939, 4 days after the 17th anniversary of his election in 1922. His death also came one day before the 10th anniversary of one of the great achievements of his reign, the Lateran Treaties, which finally brought peace between the Church and the Kingdom of Italy after the plundering inflicted on the Church by the Italian Risorgimento. ## Friday, February 10, 2023
### The Death of Pius XI
“February 10th of this year, in St Peter’s square, in the first hours of the morning, groups of people stop, sadly turning their faces towards two closed windows in the Vatican Palace. Within, still in his rooms, still on his deathbed, lies Pius XI, the Pope who, on the following day, would have celebrated in the basilica the tenth anniversary of the Reconciliation (_between the Church and the kingdom of Italy_), an anniversary very dear to his heart. Now, the body, clothed in solemn vestments, is in the Sistine Chapel, which is destined to see, in the tradition of the church of Rome, both the deceased pope, and a few days later, the first exaltation of his successor. A long procession of ecclesiastics and dignitaries accompanies the body from the Sistine Chapel to St Peter’s; outside, the throng which grows ever more crowded in the piazza seems to follow the sad ceremony in sentiment. (_no narration from 1:15 to 3:10_) Then, the gates of the basilica are opened; the mortal remains of Pius XI, before they are laid in the tomb, remain exposed for three days for the veneration of the faithful. Passing in endless lines before the body, the people express a unanimous tribute of grief to the Pope of the Reconciliation.”

Pope Pius XI (1857-1939) (original name Ambrogio Damiano Achille Ratti) , was born in Desio, Lombardy, Austrian Empire [now in Italy]. His father owned a silk factory. He was ordained a priest in 1879 and embarked on an academic career within the Church. His scholarly specialty was as an expert paleographer, a student of ancient and medieval Church manuscripts. After many years as a researcher at a Catholic library, Ratti was made Papal nuncio to Poland in 1918, then cardinal and archbishop of Milan in 1921, and then Pope in the following year.

It rejected both unrestrained economic individualism and socialism, and it criticized the concentration of economic power in a few hands.
The encyclical is best known for its statement of the principle of subsidiarity. On this principle, larger bodies, including the state, should not take over tasks that smaller communities such as families, associations, and local bodies can perform themselves; higher authority should support and assist the lower rather than absorb it. The encyclical also proposed that society be organized through vocational groups that would bring together employers and workers in each branch of the economy. Fascist Italy claimed that its own corporative system put similar ideas into practice, but the Italian state's corporations were tools of government control, and the encyclical itself voiced concern about that kind of arrangement.
Other encyclicals addressed family and education. _Divini illius magistri_ (1929) set out the Catholic understanding of Christian education, holding that the family and the church have rights in education that come before those of the state, and opposing a state monopoly over schooling. _Casti connubii_ (1930) defended the permanence of marriage and condemned artificial contraception, a teaching that later popes reaffirmed.

## Catholic Action and the laity
Pius XI made the organized lay movement known as Catholic Action a central feature of his program. He described it as the participation of the laity in the apostolate of the hierarchy: lay Catholics, organized by age, sex, and occupation, would work under the direction of the bishops to bring Christian principles into public life, the professions, and the workplace. The movement spread widely in Italy, Belgium, France, Latin America, and elsewhere.
Catholic Action became a point of conflict with the Fascist government, which wanted a monopoly over the organization of young people. When the regime moved against Catholic youth groups in 1931, Pius answered with the encyclical _Non abbiamo bisogno_ ("We do not need"), written in Italian rather than the customary Latin. In it he protested against the persecution of Catholic Action and rejected the claim of the totalitarian state to the whole of a young person's life. A compromise allowed the groups to continue under restrictions.

## Concordats and relations with states
Pius used concordats extensively to secure the church's legal position after World War I redrew the map of Europe. Agreements were reached with, among others, Latvia (1922), Bavaria (1924), Poland (1925), Lithuania (1927), Romania (1927), Prussia (1929), Italy (1929), Baden (1932), and Austria (1933). In July 1933 the Holy See signed a concordat with the German Reich, negotiated on the Vatican side by Cardinal Eugenio Pacelli, his secretary of state from 1930. It guaranteed certain rights to the church in Germany in exchange for the withdrawal of clergy from party politics. Historians continue to debate whether the agreement protected German Catholics or lent the new Nazi regime respectability; the regime in any case violated it repeatedly.
In France, diplomatic relations with the Holy See had been restored under Benedict XV in 1921, after a break of nearly two decades. Pius XI built on this by accepting, in 1924, a legal arrangement for French dioceses that allowed the church to hold property under the laws separating church and state. In 1926 he condemned the right-wing nationalist movement Action Française, whose Catholic supporters had made it a significant force in French Catholic life, because of its subordination of religion to politics.
The church faced open persecution in several countries during his reign. He protested against the anticlerical measures of the Mexican government that led to the Cristero uprising of 1926–29 and its aftermath, against the treatment of the church under the Spanish Republic and during the Spanish Civil War, and against the suppression of religion in the Soviet Union.

**Pius XI**
Pope Pius XI (1857-1939) (original name Ambrogio Damiano Achille Ratti) , was born in Desio, Lombardy, Austrian Empire [now in Italy]. His father owned a silk factory. He was ordained a priest in 1879 and embarked on an academic career within the Church. He obtained three doctorates (in philosophy, canon law and theology) at the Gregorian University in Rome, and then from 1882 to 1888 was a professor at the seminary in Padua. His scholarly specialty was as an expert paleographer, a student of ancient and medieval Church manuscripts. After many years as a researcher at a Catholic library, Ratti was made Papal nuncio to Poland in 1918, then cardinal and archbishop of Milan in 1921, and then Pope in the following year.
Among his papal encyclicals, Pius XI is most remembered for lending the support of the Church to Distributism and Subsidiarity in Quadragesimo Anno. It was promulgated in 1931 to mark ‘forty years’ since Pope Leo XIII’s (1878–1903) encyclical De Rerum Novarum. It restated that encyclical’s support for intermediating social associations and warnings against both socialism and unrestrained capitalism as enemies to human freedom and dignity.
The following excerpt defined the principle of subsidiarity that has been a feature of Catholic thought ever since:
“The State authorities should leave to other bodies the care and expediting of business and activities of lesser moment, which otherwise become for it a source of great distraction. It will then perform with greater freedom, vigor and effectiveness, the tasks belonging properly to it, and which alone it can accomplish, directing, supervising, encouraging, restraining, as circumstances suggest or necessity demands. Let those in power, therefore, be convinced that the more faithfully this principle of subsidiarity is followed and a hierarchical order prevails among the various organizations the more excellent will be the authority and efficiency of society, and the happier and more prosperous the condition of the commonwealth.”
**In Centesimus Annus (1991) John Paul II formulated the principle with a different emphasis:**

# Quadragesimo Anno
“A community of a higher order should not interfere in the internal life of a community of lower order, depriving the latter of its functions, but rather should support it in case of need and help to coordinate its activity with the activities of the rest of society, always with a view to the common good.”
